name: 5-HTP (oxitriptan)

lead: 5-HTP is the step between tryptophan and serotonin and is sold as a supplement, often for sleep and mood.
Human trials exist across several conditions, but the sources reviewed do not report their outcomes, and none targets appearance.

paras: It crosses the blood-brain barrier and is converted to serotonin; decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa raise its effect.
Serotonin syndrome is a documented concern with serotonin-raising drugs. No FDA-approved medicine contains it as of 2025.

lead: 5-Hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP), medically oxitriptan, is a naturally occurring amino acid and intermediate in serotonin synthesis. The body makes it from tryptophan via tryptophan hydroxylase, the rate-limiting step, and unlike serotonin it crosses the blood-brain barrier [1]. Food contains only insignificant amounts [1].

It is sold as a supplement for mood and sleep and is catalogued here as a sleep and recovery aid. Wikipedia states that, as of 2025, no FDA-approved medicines contain 5-HTP [1]. Registered human trials have examined it for depression, mood, body composition, fatigue, satiety and sleep, though outcome data are not summarised in the sources used.
infobox: Made from tryptophan; trace amounts in food [1]

paras: 5-HTP is converted quickly to serotonin by decarboxylation, with vitamin B6 involved [1]. Peripheral decarboxylase inhibitors such as carbidopa or benserazide increase its effects, and an investigational oxitriptan/carbidopa combination exists [1]. Older animal pharmacology work used 5-HTP to probe serotonin receptor behaviours in rodents [2].

Serotonin syndrome, with hallucinations, has been reported with overdoses of serotonin-elevating drugs [1]. In rodents very high doses cause a head-twitch response considered a proxy for psychedelic effect, but 5-HTP is not reported to produce psychedelic effects in people [1].

ClinicalTrials.gov lists human studies of 5-HTP including nutritional supplementation on sleep quality in older adults [3], body composition [4], cortisol and exercise [5], mood and emotional processing in healthy volunteers [6], satiety in obesity [7], fatigue in inflammatory bowel disease remission [8], major depression combined with creatine [9], ADHD traits [10], asthma in children [11] and spinal cord injury [12]. The sources used do not report their results, so this article draws no conclusion about effectiveness. No registered study found tests it for appearance outcomes.
